items.title: Silent Hill: Townfall Review
items.author: Tristan Ogilvie
items.content:
I spent so much of my time stalking through Silent Hill: Townfall tensed in a cautious crouchwalk, that by the end of the story I was just as worried about the damage to my character’s fraying mental state as I was about the wear and tear on his knees. Taking an about-face from the action-heavy adventure in last year’s Silent Hill f, this latest survival horror spin-off instead embraces the sustained tension of slow-paced stealth, handing you a motion-sensing gadget and tasking you with sneaking past a series of sound-sensitive beasts that have descended on its abandoned seaside village in mid-nineties Scotland. What unfolds is a gripping investigation through an increasingly unsettling world witnessed from a fresh, first-person perspective. Silent Hill: Townfall is riddled with tremendously satisfying puzzles to solve, and peppered with the most disturbing scenes to come out of mid-nineties Scotland since that baby crawled along the ceiling in the original Trainspotting.

Silent Hill: Townfall’s story begins with a cold open in more ways than one. American Simon Ordell washes up on the chilly shores of the fictional St. Amelia with a hospital ID bracelet on one wrist and an IV drip still stuck in the other, seemingly seeking redemption for an unknown sin from his past. It quickly becomes apparent that things have gone very wrong in the deserted Scottish town – market stalls are abandoned, ‘for sale’ signs are pegged out the front of almost every house, and the streets are littered with picket signs protesting an unknown organisation dubbed the ‘CEG’. Oh, and the first local you encounter is a mysterious man in the town square getting disgusting black goop pumped into his lungs through an intubation tube descending from the skies above.

Things only get more alarming from there, but Townfall dragged me through its increasingly squeamish scenes with the powerful allure of its central mystery, which gradually brings to light the tragic events that have impacted the town, the main players at fault, and exactly where poor Simon stands in all of it. It’s a story that deals with familiar themes of trauma and guilt that we’ve come to expect from Silent Hill, but it also tackles previously unexplored shades of evil like corporate greed and environmental mismanagement that help to make it feel like a refreshingly new twist on the series’ formula.

Although he comes across as fairly monotone at first, I grew to appreciate the understated earnestness of Simon as the events of Townfall mine the full depths of his despair, especially compared to some of the overly dramatic heroes of the earlier Silent Hill games. At certain junctions, the story also switches the perspective to a couple of other playable characters that further flesh out the details of what’s really going on, but I’d rather not spoil exactly who they are other than to say that they provide crucial roles in unravelling St. Amelia’s secrets.

Townfall dragged me through its increasingly squeamish scenes with the powerful allure of its central mystery.

Of course, a lot of its story themes are revealed in the form of nightmarish visual metaphors, as St. Amelia shifts into an ominous altered state with tangles of industrial pipes strangling its streets and the tentacles of a towering monster that drag along its rooftops. Sure, some sections feel like echoes of earlier Silent Hill settings, like apartment blocks in a heavy state of decay and creepy hospital wards to explore, but there are some really striking new sights to see throughout the 13 hours of Townfall’s tragic tale too, from alleys cloaked in a crimson haze to suburban streets lined with horribly bloated corpses that have freshly fallen from the sky.

The fact that developer Screen Burn Games has opted to break from the series’ predominately third-person style by telling its story entirely in first-person also does wonders for enhancing Townfall’s overall sense of dread. As proven by Resident Evil’s modern instalments, it’s considerably more intimidating to lean around a corner and come face to gaping maw with a menacing manifestation of pure malevolence than it is to witness it from a comparatively safe distance peering over your character’s shoulder. However, Townfall further enhances its first-person view by defaulting its presentation to a letterboxed widescreen format, and the benefits are twofold; aside from lending it a welcome cinematic touch, its narrowed anamorphic perspective also makes moving through confined spaces feel all the more claustrophobic and uncomfortable.

Whereas last year’s Silent Hill f demanded that you master an aggressive, action RPG-style melee and parry system, Townfall encourages a slow and steady approach to its enemy encounters that feels more inline with the survival horror systems of the series’ mainline entries. Simon can get his hands on wooden two-by-fours and lead pipes in order to beat the black pudding out of his frenzied assailants, but the actual melee combat is intentionally sluggish and weapons can degrade and break. More often than not, that meant I opted to sneak past the snarling skinbags patrolling the path to my next objective, only ever choosing violence when I found myself backed into a corner.

Even when you eventually do get your hands on some more powerful weapons like the revolver and shotgun, ammunition remains scarce, reload times are realistically slow, and the booming echo of gunfire tends to attract attention from other enemies. This makes them primarily last resort options when you find yourself overwhelmed by fleshmonsters with axe-blades for faces that are frantically trying to give you a Glasgow kiss.

Thankfully the environment provides you with enough tools to allow for a passive approach. As was the case in The Last of Us series, house bricks and empty bottles can be lobbed to create distractions away from your position, or thrown directly at an enemy to momentarily stun them and allow you to scurry past. Devices like radios can also be switched on to lure shuffling sentries away from their stations, and should you get spotted, there’s usually a conveniently placed wardrobe somewhere close by for you to run and hide in. Just be sure to break the line of sight before you do – if one of the unkillable stalker enemy types spots you cowering in a cupboard, it’s liable to rip you right out of there like the xenomorph from Alien: Isolation and send you straight back to your last save point.

Speaking of Alien: Isolation, Townfall reimagines the iconic motion tracker device from Creative Assembly’s sci-fi scarefest in the form of a portable TV that Simon clutches in his left hand. Bursts of static alert you to the presence of any nasties that might lurk in the murk ahead, and by tuning the little frequency band on his CRTV-branded device you can dial in a slightly glitchy, sonar-style view of their position on its tiny LCD screen, allowing you to plan your next steps through each area accordingly. You can’t keep a bead on every enemy at the same time, however, since each of Townfall’s monsters occupy their own space on the CRTV’s band. Anytime I found myself in more densely populated areas, I was forced to constantly flick through the frequencies in order to identify the nearest threat, which further ratcheted up my stress levels.

That said, although the CRTV is a vital piece of kit for surviving the increasingly mean streets of St. Amelia, its ability to effectively see through walls and allow you to anticipate any monsters waiting to ambush you means that Townfall is pretty light on any substantial scares in its opening hours. It eventually found a way to jolt me with a few excellent jump scares later on, especially during the prolonged section that removes the CRTV from your inventory and forces you to contend with an office block full of ghouls that stand statue-like in the shadows before surprising you when you turn away. Yet even though Townfall might not ever come close to the underwear-changing chills of the Silent Hill 2 remake or the heart-stopping horrors of Grace’s levels in Resident Evil Requiem, it does use its consistently unsettling atmosphere to maintain a strong feeling of unease throughout.

The CRTV isn’t just a handy way to keep tabs on Townfall’s terrors, it’s also a valuable tool for uncovering clues to your next objective. Cryptic looping videos will often pierce through the static and offer brief glimpses of a specific location, forcing you to carefully scan your surroundings rather than blindly following a simple map marker to reach it. However, the CRTV isn’t the only relic from the ‘90s that you get your hands on in Townfall, since so many of the story’s puzzles involve operating all sorts of other obsolete technologies from the decade like cream-coloured desktop computers and slide projectors, each recreated with convincing effect right down to the rhythmic mechanical screeches of a dot matrix printer.

Anyone who played this developer’s 2017 debut Stories Untold (released under the studio’s previous name, No Code) will be familiar with the team’s ability to accurately replicate the look and feel of such bygone gadgets and gizmos – and as someone nostalgic for the era, I got a kick out of methodically loading floppy disks into a drive in order to unzip important documents, or the tactile experience of manually punching a series of digits into the metal keypad of a public payphone to save my game. This may well sound a bit mundane to you if you’re not old enough to remember monochrome monitors, but don’t worry because these primitive pieces of tech are occasionally used to trigger some seriously surreal sequences. For example, a microcassette recorder I found in one abandoned residence could be used to shuffle the contents of the house back and forward through time, opening up slightly altered areas to scour for a specific puzzle solution and briefly bending my mind into a pretzel.

I respect that for the most part the clues you need to solve each of Townfall’s brainteasers are there to find in your immediate surroundings as long as you’re prepared to search for them, and also the fact that in some instances there are countermeasures for any attempts to brute force your way to a solution. For example, in one level where you’re guided through the process of prepping a patient for surgery by a condescending doctor on the other end of an intercom, it soon turns into a sadistic game of Operation when identifying the wrong readout on a life support system triggers a health bar-sapping buzz. That really forced me to focus on finding the right solution, and when I applied myself I discovered Townfall’s puzzles to be regularly challenging but rarely too obtuse.

That is, aside from one particular late game contraption that confounded me so much that it seemed as though Silent Hill’s signature fog had seeped into my own brain. Seriously, it made me feel like I was Homer Simpson sitting at his keyboard and searching for the ‘ANY’ key. (It’s worth pointing out, though, that if you prefer to have your brain gently tickled rather than outright teased, you can activate hints in the options menu.)

Lastly, I was happy to find that Silent Hill: Townfall wasn’t ever dragged down by the same inventory management issues I encountered in Silent Hill f. Unlike the miserly nature of the item slots in last year’s spin-off, Townfall doesn’t really place restrictions on what you can carry besides limiting you to two throwable items and one melee weapon at any one time. You can otherwise hold as much ammunition and medkits as you like, although given how scarce these resources are it’s typically only ever a handful at any one time anyway.

One particular late game puzzle confounded me so much that it seemed as though Silent Hill’s signature fog had seeped into my own brain.

There’s a light amount of crafting, too, since you can sterilise regular bandages with bottles of alcohol in order to make them more effective healing options. Meanwhile, the ability to fill an IV bag with revitalising fluid and keep it constantly equipped proved essential (especially as enemy numbers swelled in the story’s final hours) since it brings you back to life with a partially refilled health bar anytime you’re downed. Aside from some rare exceptions when I was killed by an enemy, brought back to life on the spot, and then instantly killed by the same enemy again before I had a chance to flee or fight back, I appreciated having the safety net of the IV drip since it gave me the courage to spend longer excursions exploring each area. That’s opposed to painstakingly tiptoeing back and forth to the nearest save point in order to bank each small amount of story progress I made, which is the cowardly path I often take in spooky stories like this.

items.title: Lanterns Season 1, Episode 6 Review & Recap
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for Lanterns Season 1, Episode 6!

It was obvious from watching Lanterns Episode 5 that the series was due for a major shake-up in the remaining three installments. The 2016 storyline reached its fiery climax, as half of Rushville was destroyed, the Manhunter stood revealed, and John Stewart (Aaron Pierre) and Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) finally had their big falling-out. The series now pivots by returning fully to the 2026 timeline first teased in the pilot and digging into the mystery surrounding Hal's apparent murder. Lanterns is a very different show in Episode 6, and not necessarily for the better.

Looking at Season 1 as a whole so far, the pacing is definitely a little strange. Lanterns teased a 2026 narrative early on and then waited a full month to return to that plot thread. Meanwhile, you have Episode 5 acting as a major storytelling climax smack dab in the middle of the narrative. I can't help but wonder if there might have been some way to more evenly divvy up the 2016 and 2026 storylines and delay the epic battle in Rushville till later in the season. To be fair, I can only imagine the extra challenges that would impose on the writers. How do you dig deeper into 2026 without overtly spoiling what happens in 2016?

And as it stands, it sounds like Episode 5 was originally intended to be Episode 7, so there was certainly some experimentation going on with the season's structure. It's just a difficult adjustment going from the spectacle and drama of Episode 5 to this quieter, more somber murder mystery in Episode 6. It's like riding a rollercoaster that peaks midway through.

The real problem with the 10-year jump forward, though, is that we lose out on the show's biggest selling point. Hal being dead means we don't get that all-important dynamic between the two Green Lanterns. Episode 6 only really has the one scene between them in the diner, taking place hours before Hal is mysteriously killed. It's a great scene, mind you, with Chandler delivering some of his best work on the series to date and really conveying the decade of emotional and physical hardship Hal has endured since the two last met. We even see him show genuine fear at the thought of John revealing that they met, which opens up all sorts of burning questions. Sadly, it's just not enough.

This episode tries to make up for the lack of Hal by establishing friction between John and various other characters. His relationships with his various family members have clearly frayed over the course of 10 years, and the episode is pretty elegant at conveying all that backstory without becoming overly expository. There's also the idea that John is wading into dangerous waters by returning to Rushville and implicating himself in Hal's murder. This is becoming a portrait of a man trying to prevent his carefully constructed, post-superhero life from falling apart.

But try as it might, Episode 6 doesn't fully hook me in that regard. Particuarly when it comes to the subplot involving the waitress Maggie (Hannah Christine Shetler) blackmailing John, it just feels like writers Justin Britt-Gibson and Damon Lindelof are adding character drama for the sake of it. I want the series to focus on the more pressing matters - the identity of Hal's killer, the whereabouts of Sinestro (Ulrich Thomsen), the question of how and why John finally embraces his destiny as the Green Lantern. Placing so much emphasis on John's legal troubles and efforts to salvage his architecture firm just comes across as a narrative diversion.

Apart from the early diner scene, Episode 6 mainly succeeds when it focuses more on the Green Lantern side of things. For one thing, we finally get that long-promised cameo from Nathan Fillion's Guy Gardner. Guy helps fill that Hal-shaped hole in the series for a couple of scenes, quickly establishing a fun dynamic with John that I hope is explored more in Man of Tomorrow next year. This episode addresses some of the big questions regarding the Green Lantern successorship and why Guy, not Hal or John, was the designated Lantern in 2025's Superman.

The funeral sequence also works very well, serving as a bleakly amusing little tribute to Hal and an exploration of how far the character has fallen over the years. Hal assumed his funeral would be attended by dignitaries and celebrities both terrestrial and alien, and yet the only people who show up are two old girlfriends and one ex-colleague who hated his guts. On that note, it's a nice treat to see Carol Ferris (Amie MacKenzie) stop by and allude to her own tumultuous history with Hal. But as with a lot of the classic Green Lantern supporting characters in this show, we don't really get enough of Carol before she's gone.

All in all, Episode 6 is a fairly disappointing follow-up to the stellar "Lights Out," but I'm hopeful things will pick up in Episode 7. The fact that the Halogram is back in action means the show can get back to emphasizing the terrific chemistry between Pierre and Chandler. The series just needs to focus more on the story threads that truly matter.

items.title: Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story Review
items.author: Jim Vejvoda
items.content:
Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story is now streaming on Netflix. This review contains spoilers.

“Sometimes I wonder did she really do these things? Or is it just a story with embellishments? Could people really be that cruel back then?” Lizzie Borden (Ella Beatty) asks this of her housemaid/lover Bridget "Maggie" Sullivan () as they read about Countess Elizabeth Báthory. It’s just one of the many on-the-nose moments in Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story, the fourth installment in Ryan Murphy and Ian Brennan’s true crime Netflix franchise.

This season explores the 1892 murders of wealthy Andrew Borden (Charlie Hunnam) and his wife Abby (Rebecca Hall) in Fall River, Massachusetts. Andrew’s youngest daughter Lizzie is tried for their murders but acquitted by an all-male jury thanks largely to shoddy police work and the belief that a woman was incapable of committing such a heinous, violent crime. Those are the basic facts of the Borden case.

Showrunner Ian Brennan, who wrote all eight episodes, invents pretty much everything else in this clumsy exploration of, in his words, “.” That’s why two other real-life infamous women – the aforementioned Blood Countess (also played by Krieps) and serial killer Aileen Wuornos (Sarah Paulson) – are shoehorned into what is a show about Lizzie Borden. Brennan wants the viewer to know that women have always had it bad, as if that’s a shocking new revelation. Monster’s not as philosophical or smart as it thinks it is, declaring its message loudly but often with the depth of a virtue-signaling social media post.

The truth about the Lizzie Borden case is that we simply don’t know the truth of what happened or why. Lizzie’s story changed multiple times. Monster, though, never doubts her guilt. The show opens with her killing her father and stepmother. It’s a whydunit not a whodunit. While subtlety is not really to be expected from any production that bears Ryan Murphy’s name, at least consistency would be appreciated.

Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story begins as camp, its first episodes directed by Max Winkler with such rapid-fire theatricality that Baz Luhrmann would need a breather. (Winkler also works in some Wes Anderson-esque compositions at times.) That tone doesn’t match with the two episodes directed by Sarah Adina Smith, whose episodes are among the stronger ones this season. I wonder if binge-watchers will stick with The Lizzie Borden Story through those zanier early episodes in order to get to Smith’s.

The over-the-top performances by Rebecca Hall and Charlie Hunnam initially portray the murder victims as undeserving of any sympathy at all. The show wants the viewer to see them get what’s coming to them. Later, Abby and Andrew each get their own episode that humanizes them enough that you understand why they became the people they did, so that when their murders are revisited the viewer is being asked (a bit too late) to have mixed feelings about what Lizzie, with Maggie’s assistance, does to them.

As a stepmother more wicked than any Disney animated movie could conjure, Hall milks every contemptuous line in Abby’s many cruel putdowns, wielding words as sharp as the axes Andrew keeps. Hunnam’s boorish, stammering Andrew oozes with disdain for women, drowning his sorrows with booze and affairs until he becomes a Jack Torrance-like maniac in his final moments (before literally seeing the light).

"Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story strains to jam a modern overlay onto its period story. 

Both Beatty and Krieps do what they can with the material they’ve been given, but they can’t elevate it. Beatty’s blank-eyed, timid Lizzie evolves into a more cunning and confident young woman through her romantic relationship with Maggie. Alas, there’s no evidence either way if Lizzie and Maggie were lovers. The show omits Maggie’s testimony at Lizzie’s trial, and also largely erases Maggie’s Irishness to accommodate the Luxembourg-born Krieps, with her aged-up character garbed like a Victorian Annie Hall.

In a household where a maid gets her face scalded over making the wrong soup, we’re supposed to believe Maggie could come to work at the home of the richest man in town with purple hair and keep her job? You couldn’t even go to work at an office like that in the 1980s let alone in the 1890s. I bring this up as an illustration of how much Monster: The Lizzie Borden Story strains to jam a modern overlay onto its period story.

The contemporary portions of this season, where it follows Aileen Wuornos, is where Monster has a better grasp on what it’s trying to say about feminine rage. You can’t take your eyes off Paulson’s Wuornos, although there are a few comedic moments in the “Bed & Breakfast” episode where she comes perilously close to channeling Kate McKinnon’s “Colleen Rafferty” character from SNL.

While Wuornos’ fascination with Lizzie and her trip to the Borden home is entirely fictional, the final episode made me wish this season had just been about Aileen Wuornos with Lizzie Borden as the side story. Or, Wuornos’ story could have been its own standalone season of Monster, in which case The Lizzie Borden Story might have benefited from having a shorter, more focused story that allowed itself to pick a tone and stick to it.

items.title: EA Sports FC 27 Review So Far
items.author: Michael Higham
items.content:
I find myself in a weird place for my in-progress review of EA Sports FC 27. On one hand, worthwhile strategic elements have finally been added that reflect real-world tactics in a concise, intuitive way. On the other hand, the promised improvements to behavior and pathing of computer-controlled players on the field still ring hollow, carrying over many of the same issues the series has had for over a decade. Couple this with the dreaded introduction of open-world elements via The Grounds, and the result is yet another instance of positive steps forward but negative steps backward.

Ever since NBA 2K14 introduced MyPark, which eventually evolved into The Neighborhood in NBA 2K18 and The City in NBA 2K21, I figured it was only a matter of time before EA brought a similar open world full of activities to its sports franchises. While The Grounds isn't without merit, it often feels like EA is trying to solve a problem that didn't really exist.

My first impression is that The Grounds doesn’t need to be an open-world environment to deliver what the playerbase wants out of a more communal online mode. I don’t need to run through a visually saturated, low-resolution city populated by lifeless NPCs just to find a game mode to start up when simple menus devoted to the same function can do the same thing in a more efficient manner. Sure, it works well as an active lobby for matchmaking and makes it easier to find other players and move between activities, but between the framerate drops and unnatural character animations, nothing immersed me in the hub in EA Sports FC 27 enough to justify its existence.

The issues above are only compounded by the myriad of unskippable cutscenes and NBA 2K15-level voice acting that make up The Grounds. The irony is that I was initially excited by the new hub world because it brings back one of my favorite FIFA characters from The Journey story mode: Alex Hunter, who first appeared in FIFA 17 and FIFA 18, once again voiced by Adetomiwa Edun. That enthusiasm disappeared quickly once Hunter began speaking, as his delivery feels noticeably more rigid and detached than it did during his original story.

The Grounds often feels like EA is trying to solve a problem that didn't really exist.

Edun's performance nearly a decade ago was passionate and natural, whereas The Grounds' version of Hunter sounds like he would rather be anywhere else. Things get even more painful when Kylian Mbappe appears shortly afterward, delivering his lines with such a stiff, mechanical cadence that it was clear he read his lines directly from a script all in one take. I honestly found myself grateful that my created character doesn't speak to avoid adding more uncomfortable interactions. While I plan to explore more of the online portion of The Grounds this weekend, the hub itself has not made a particularly strong first impression.

When it comes to gameplay, EA Sports FC 27's expanded Tactics system is easily the best addition, wonderfully complementing the playstyles and roles introduced over the past few years. The new strategy system gives much more control over how teams behave in different phases of play, going beyond basic formations and instructions by explaining the purpose, strengths, and weaknesses of different tactical approaches. This becomes particularly useful when building around individual player attributes. As a Manchester United fan, I found that a deeper defensive approach worked especially well for Noussair Mazraoui, whose patient style lets him maintain his position and disrupt attacks without constantly stepping out of shape, while a short-passing buildup gives him chances to use his technical ability without abandoning that defensive structure.

That flexibility became even more apparent when I switched formations on the fly mid-match while playing against Crystal Palace – I found that they were leaving space along the wings, so I moved into a 4-2-2-2, letting Bruno Fernandes operate between the lines and thread passes to a striker such as Benjamin Sesko, creating opportunities for quick combinations and finishes through the middle. Alternatively, when I faced Manchester City, they controlled the wings more successfully. To counter this, I switched to a 4-2-3-1 wide formation, moving Fernandes more centrally so he dictates play and combines with holding midfielders such as Kobbie Mainoo through quick one-two passes.

Separating tactical instructions for possession and defensive phases adds another useful layer, while Player Roles give individual players more specific responsibilities within a formation. Instead of simply placing someone in a position and expecting them to behave a certain way, I can now build their role around the specific contribution I want from them. For example, if I move into a 4-2-3-1 wide and place Benjamin Šeško on the right side, I can adjust his role depending on the circumstances. As an inside forward, he can cut inward to create shooting opportunities or provide another passing option for Fernandes, while a wider role allows him to stretch the defense and open space through the middle.

That same flexibility can be useful defensively, particularly when protecting a lead. If an opponent repeatedly targets his side of the pitch, giving Šeško more defensive responsibility lets him drop back and support the right back, providing another way to protect that flank without abandoning the attacking structure. What makes the system particularly valuable is that it teaches the strategy behind soccer formations without overwhelming players with unnecessary information. EA Sports FC 27 does a good job explaining why different shapes work, which players suit them, and how to adjust them against different opponents, making the tactical aspect for the sport approachable while still leaving experienced players plenty of room to experiment.

When it comes to gameplay, EA Sports FC 27's expanded Tactics system is easily the best addition.

The biggest issue is that the tactical system can sometimes feel like it is working against the game's own computer-controlled behavior. Pathing and defensive logic can still break down on higher difficulties, allowing a carefully constructed gameplan to be undermined by an CPU defender refusing to challenge for a 50/50 ball or making an inexplicable movement. Passing will still occasionally produce similarly frustrating results when a ball aimed toward an open teammate on the right is instead sent toward a covered player in the middle.

Crossing and corner kicks have also improved noticeably, with both systems producing more convincing positioning battles and giving the player greater control over what happens inside the box. I scored several successful headers with Harry Maguire from corners during my time with the game, which stood out because I could count on one hand the number of corner routines and headed goals I had scored in previous EA Sports FC entries.

I'm going to explore Career Mode, Presentation, Online, and Ultimate Team, and dive deeper into how Tactics will affect both single-player and multiplayer modes, in the coming days before locking in my full scored review – stay tuned.

items.title: Control Resonant Review
items.author: Michael Higham
items.content:
Paranatural phenomena, Objects of Power, and interdimensional threats all defying the laws of physics – developer Remedy has built its reputation on these kinds of concepts, and none more intriguing than the fantastic Control in 2019. The subtleties in its SCP-adjacent mysteries are what left a lasting impact, so in many regards, Control Resonant is an antithesis. Not only has the series moved from metroidvania-esque shooter to open-world stylish-action, it also goes for a more straightforward story focused on the lives of its characters. It's not always elegant in its action, and can even range from frustrating to somewhat dull in certain stretches. Still, I came away impressed by how conceptually consistent it is with Control while also being radically different. Remedy could've played it safe, but Control Resonant dares to be bold where it counts, with swings that land alongside some of this studio's best.

Control Resonant is centered around Dylan Faden, the brother of the first game's lead Jesse Faden, who backflipped into becoming the director of the Federal Bureau of Control, and it uses his perspective to fill in a lot blanks from the jump. He goes from being Jesse's tortured brother who was the subject of abusive FBC experiments gone awry to a fully formed character with thoughts, feelings, and dark memories he confronts as he tries to salvage whatever life he has left. He's treated as subhuman and initially seen as dangerous with superpowers he can't always ,but still volunteers to be a tool of the FBC with what's effectively a shock collar bolted onto the back of his head.

With this as the foundation, Control Resonant treats much of its paranatural conspiracy as a matter of fact. The Oldest House couldn't contain the Hiss outbreak as it spills into a New York City that's been folded in on itself in interdimensional isolation, which turns out to be a swift and effective setup as Dylan tries to find Jesse, who's been lost over the last seven years. And while this story does expand on what we know about things like the Hiss and AWEs, it resonates more as an exploration about what you would do in the aftermath of a life and world fallen apart.

Your search mostly comes in the form of physically dismantling paranormal entities and the monsters they spawn, which have filled the streets, with up-close and personal combat. Dylan himself contrasts with Jesse in that he plays fast and nimble with a suite of melee combos and abilities that he was specifically built for. Similar to Jesse's shapeshifting gun, Dylan's melee weapon called the Aberrant transforms into whatever form you either assign to it or combo into. The Aberrant can be a sword, scythe, hammer, or even a drill, but instead of equipping these as individual pieces of gear, it automatically swaps forms depending on whether you're doing a light combo chain, heavy attack, or a combo finisher. All of this can be customized to suit your preferred playstyle as you expand in power and capability through upgrade trees, giving a level of variability I appreciate.

The action is slick and responsive like a Devil May Cry or Bayonetta, with of the platforming and momentum I miss from Gravity Rush or NieR: Automata. If I'm mid-combo but need to dodge immediately, I can cancel out of the animation with a dash/airdash and pick the combo back up so long as I don't get hit. Grasping this cadence of character-action is paramount because you will die a lot in the early hours. The kid gloves come off very quickly, and part of the difficulty is a consequence of not having many tools to pull from initially, but enemies hit hard and are oftentimes relentless with just how much they throw at you. It can be frustrating when you're on the verge of conquering a combat encounter, so there's an element of chaos management to consider.

Control Resonant's RPG edge is the equalizer here, offering progression and some build crafting through both Dylan's own skill tree and weapon upgrades paths. Some of my favorite powers were as satisfying as they were effective, like summoning a minion that I can throw like a massive bomb to inflict significant Falter damage (this game's stagger meter) and clear mobs of pesky Hiss. Once I unlocked the Ignite power that let me set weapons ablaze to quickly inflict Burn status and melt enemies into piles of Faltered targets to execute, the action changed significantly. Instead of feeling vulnerable and picking my windows of opportunity to strike, Dylan became the real threat as my Spin Edge combo and Hammer charge scorched anything that was once deadly. (It also helped that Ignite sheds off mold poison, which gave me so much trouble early on.)

There are status effects that are important to account for, but it did feel a bit like I had found the "correct" build. Even though that took away some of the need to be incisive in combat, I can't deny that it was pretty sweet to play things more like a hack-and-slash just by virtue of understanding how to wield its systems. So, the RPG aspect isn't quite as deep as it looks at first glance since your approach won't drastically evolve at a certain point and the combo system doesn't change much, but the fundamentals are there.

Combat is designed to encourage and reward aggression, with every killed enemy dropping health and each melee attack feeding back into the power meter you use for special abilities. That philosophy is also seen in the design of most encounters, which are primarily built around killing heavy enemies since they continuously spawn minions in the combat arenas that form as you explore. Trying to whittle down mobs is sometimes wasted effort, you just have to go for the big ones and treat the rest like obstacles or a way to replenish health if you can wedge a combo in there unscathed.

The handful of bosses you'll find in story quests, are quite striking and most of them play extremely well into the otherworldlyness of Control's phasing realities. Their attack patterns and movesets aren't anything out of the ordinary for action games of this style, but their unsettling and imposing presence is certainly seen and felt. However, encounter design is where Control Resonant falters most. Roughly half the bosses are spongy slogs that are less about testing your mastery and more about grinding out a war of attrition. Once you see their handful of tricks, you just have to rinse and repeat as you chip away at their health bar and hope you don't trip up in the repetitive cycle that it demands from you. A few later bosses also leaned heavily into aerial combat against faster moving targets, which was curious as its systems weren't exactly built for this type of encounter. Dylan can glide like using a hookshot, airdash, hover temporarily, and hit an air combo, but when you combine this with floating platforms and a targeting system that doesn't reliably agree with the camera, it chipped at my enthusiasm.

I kept pace with progression, which revolves around levelling up your status in each zone afforded by main missions and side activities alike. And I upgraded the Aberrant accordingly to raise its overall power level while seeking out optional health and power capacity upgrades judiciously. So, I didn't exactly feel noticeably underpowered for most of the 30-hour journey, and that makes hitting walls like these so jarring. I've loved the challenge that came with games like Sekiro or Devil May Cry V on Dante Must Die difficulty, and those deftly demand precise execution and sharp focus – Control Resonant doesn't always define challenge in interesting ways. It's undercooked in spots, but that doesn't sour everything around it. So frustrations aside, Remedy's first crack at this style of action combat is admirable because its foundationally sound and does have satisfying moments that the genre greats pull off.

Control Resonant strikes a delicate balance, letting the world itself take the lead rather than waypointing every little thing.

Where Control Resonant really shines is in the mind-bending, gravity-defying world Remedy built for it. You're not going to find your local bodega in the Lower East Side or the 4-train to Harlem in this version of Manhattan. However, the way the design language of The Oldest House has spilled into the streets gives it a personality that's so distinctly Control. The environment seamlessly guides you on what's what and where to go, so even in the absence of a more detailed map, I was rarely ever lost as long as I paid attention to my surroundings. This strikes a delicate balance, letting the world itself take the lead rather than waypointing every little thing.

Deeper in, you'll be able to shift Dylan's gravitational center in parts of the map, and it quite literally adds an extra dimension that is both visually brain-breaking and a marvel in level design. Those strange areas where city streets shoot upward or solid ground is oddly above you – yeah, those are other planes waiting to be explored. Sometimes combat shifts between these planes in the same encounter, which occasionally had my head spinning (mostly complimentary). The Gravity Rush of it all plays a major role in how you move through late-game zones as the feeling of falling through the sky creates a unique thrill outside of combat. And when you start to understand how these various planes converge and break from each other, I can only envy the genius of how it was designed and the headache it must have been to create, especially at this scope and scale. It's not just for show; even when it gets unwieldy, it adds depth and texture to what would've felt like a fairly standard world.

There are more than just checklist objectives to find as you explore these spaces as well, though I don't mind a sprinkling of typical open-world activities when navigation itself is part of the joy. While side content and the rewards it provides aren’t always particularly interesting, there's usually something enticing to glean about the psychological toll AWEs have had on survivors. For example, strange taxi cabs found in each zone take you to an alternate realm for a sidequest series to help a woman stuck between dimensions. Here, you essentially play multiple sequences of minigames that are as silly as they are unsettling. There are nice moments where Dylan cleans up a hangout spot people once had and sketches the scene to show his artistic side. Requiring you to physically go to fast travel points to use them(as opposed to just pulling up the map and selecting a point), you're more likely to stumble upon neat things like this and Resonant is better for it. Sometimes these moments are super goofy, sometimes they're pretty dark, and often they are both – such is the tonal contrast that is Remedy's signature.

Along with the studio's strong Lynchian vibe, what I always remember about Remedy's games are the unconventional ways they tell their stories. With this in mind, Control Resonant is interesting in how it follows more typical storytelling conventions, brushing up against tropes we've seen time and again, but still remembering why we're drawn to the Control universe. Even in Jesse's absence, her presence lingers over the story to drive Dylan's convictions and remind us of how powerful a figure she's become. Dylan is a real sad sack who feels sorry for himself, and it's quite tragic as you unpack what really happened to him as an FBC experiment. And that's what makes Dylan so compelling and easy to root for; he's not a complex character, but he is a good guy and a clear lens to demystify a lot of the esoteric concepts of Control's world.

Control Resonant's story isn't as heavily shrouded in mystery, but the things that happen within it are potentially more fascinating than ever. The way this bizzaro-world manifests during a few specific parts makes for some of its best moments – particularly in how Resonant also works seamlessly as a sort of prequel that tidies up a lot of what was either left to implication or collectible documents in Control. And man, I wish I could tell you tricks it has up its sleeve, because Resonant has some of my favorite twists in all of Remedy's work – and definitely one of the most memorable moments I've had in a game, period. Part of Dylan and Jesse's past is rooted in having video games as kids, and where this goes hit me hard as someone whose childhood was shaped by the very references made here. You'll often see games, movies, or shows make references as a gimmick that don't really go beyond “hey, look at this thing you remember!” (Take a look at the Verconn building in-game; clearly Remedy has some Evangelion fans in the building, but that's cool.) For Control Resonant to transcend that in such an effective way further speaks to Remedy's storytelling prowess.

One specific quest arc delves into alternate realities and timelines; it gets progressively more fascinating as you unravel both the science/lore behind this and how it contrasts with the human cost on its researchers. Audio tapes and documents left behind complement the Inception-like phenomenon happening in the quest, giving you enough pieces to explain things while not being overbearing, trusting that you can make sense of it all. More than being a fascinating spin on the concept, it made me feel for characters I barely got to know. It's a microcosm of how the various mechanisms and anomalies of Control's world are couched in a tight consistency.

The various mechanisms and anomalies of Control's world are couched in a tight consistency.

In the process of the FBC trying to clean up the outbreak and solve its interdimensional crisis, Dylan develops a dynamic with his quippy handler named Zoe. She plays an important and persistent role as Dylan's foil, but the shifts in their dynamic don't always feel earned, as if it just needed to accelerate to match the pace of the campaign itself. Similarly, the main story relies on a few easy logical leaps to tidy things up, which means it may not be quite as moving in the grand scheme of the Remedyverse. That leaves Control Resonant feeling like a collection of incredible moments – cohesive when strung together and powerful in what they say about characters who exist in such a deranged world, but not necessarily as effective when it comes to its central, overarching tale. Still, the humanizing element and the paranormal it is embedded within bolster each other, which helps this sequel come out the other end as a fitting part of the universe Remedy has built all the same.

items.title: Star Trek: Strange New Worlds Season 4, Episode 9 Recap and Review - It's Time for La'An Vs. La'An
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Look, I’m sure it’s a lot of fun for the actors on Strange New Worlds to get to drop the Starfleet uniforms for the week and put on exotic dresses and costumes that remind them of their salad days from their college drama programs or whatever, but it’s not as much fun for us to watch. Or, at the very least, it’s not as much fun for me. Not fun at all at this point, in fact.

So yes, “Once La’An a Time” continues Season 4’s trend of doing kooky concept episodes – I’m so sick of typing “concept episode” at this point – but not just that. It’s now doing to concept episodes from previous seasons. In this case, it’s to Season 1’s “The Elysian Kingdom,” where the crew all turned into characters from a storybook, including princesses and wizards and henchmen and warriors and so on. It was a new idea for the show at the time, and it was fun – not to mention that it was also centered on a key emotional storyline for Babs Olusanmokun’s Dr. M’Benga which involved his sick daughter.

But now we’re back at it, only this time the episode is mainly about Christina Chong’s La’An and the battle with her darker impulses that she’s been struggling with all season. And there’s no denying that Chong is typically brilliant here despite the circumstances she’s given; seeing the always-angry La’An try to cry, but proving unable to, is a hoot. And the episode, written by Onitra Johnson (who co-wrote the Season 1 episode) and directed by Sydney Freeland, eventually gets to a satisfying conclusion for the character after she literally has to face herself during the Elysian shenanigans.

And yeah, we get to see the Enterprise face off against a dragon – and be on the losing side until “magic” is deployed – which is an undeniably cool twist, and also kind of calls back to the sort of situation we might’ve seen on The Original Series if they had the budget. After all, that was a show that once gave us the giant hand of the Greek god Apollo grabbing the ship in space, and another time teamed up Captain Kirk and Mister Spock with Abraham Lincoln!

But you know, those episodes were fun, and “Once La'An a Time” is more annoying than anything else. I guess I have to keep saying this, but when you’ve got only 10 episodes per season and you continue to use that precious time to put your captain into situations where he has to act like a captain, at a certain point you’re doing the character, the actor, and the fans a disservice. And that’s where Anson Mount (and Ethan Peck this week as well) finds himself as he has to prance around the Enterprise as his other self, Sir Amand Rauth, while the real Captain Pike is stuck in a painting for most of the episode. It’s a drag and it adds up to a bunch of nothing in the end.

Paul Wesley, meanwhile, is back after last week’s crackerjack Kirk episode, but this time it’s to play Prince Dashing, the storybook love interest of La’An’s Princess Thalia. The character turns out to be a werewolf, which sure, that’s fun, but it doesn’t really amount to anything either. And the show continues to push the romance between La’An and Kirk… you know, between a descendent of Khaaaaaaaan!!!! and the future Admiral Kirk. I won’t ding the show for doing this, but I am increasingly convinced that we are unlikely to ever get any answers as to how this makes any sense in the larger canon.

Questions and Notes from the Q Continuum:

  • Somehow I’ve been spelling “La’An” as “La’an” all season. Please accept my shame and grant me forgiveness.
  • So is that a wrap for Pelia and Carol Kane? Strange New Worlds only has seven episodes left (Season 5, remember, will only be six episodes), so it’s generally been assumed that she’d be phased out and Martin Quinn’s Scotty would take over as Chief Engineer. Also, Pike says she’s flying the Elysian planet/ship “home” – does he mean Earth?
  • What happened to all the dopplegangers? Did Queen Neve (Uhura’s evil double) survive? I know they said beam her to the brig. What about Sir Amand Rauth and Wizard Pollux and the wet fart that was their storyline here? Will they pay for their transgressions?
  • Yes, the dog Runa is Christina Chong’s actual dog in real life too, Runa Ewok (amazing dog name), who she often brings to conventions and publicity events. Cute.
  • I had forgotten that Benny Russell, Captain Sisko’s alter ego from Deep Space Nine’s “Far Beyond the Stars” and “Shadows and Symbols,” was revealed to be the author of the book The Kingdom of Elysian back in Season 1. (Pelia pretends to be Benny here.) That same episode therefore established that Benny was an actual person and not a figment of Sisko’s imagination – for better or worse.

items.title: South Park Season 29 Premiere Review & Recap: "South American Biker Gangs"
items.author: Jesse Schedeen
items.content:
Warning: This review contains full spoilers for South Park Season 29, Episode 1!

Part of the fun with each new season of South Park is seeing where the series directs its attention after being off the air for months (sometimes years). It's not as if there's any shortage of big news and topical headlines worth lampooning right now. And the show certainly made a strong impression right out of the gate in last year's Season 27 premiere. That's why it's a little surprising to see Season 29 take a very different approach in its premiere episode. Despite a few nods to current events, this is very much a classic-style episode. And honestly, it makes for a nice change of pace.

Obviously, the series has hardly moved on from lampooning the actions of the Trump administration in Season 29. It's right there in the decision to change the title to "South America." And it seems safe to assume South America is going to increasingly lean into political humor as we get closer to the November midterms (and the release of GTA VI). But for now, we get an episode that really plays like a throwback to the early seasons of the show. The focus shifts back to Stan, Kyle, Cartman, and Kenny. Randy is out there being a solipsistic doofus. The episode even climaxes with Kenny dying for the first time in however many years it's been. It really is a blast from the past in many ways.

For the most part, that classical approach works well here. I do think the climax of the episode is a little rushed and unsatisfying. But for the most part, it really is a refreshing change of pace to see Stan and the gang in the spotlight again and for the show to pivot away from trying to be as superhumanly timely as possible. Cartman tends to steal the spotlight here, as his sheer glee over the freedom granted by being an obnoxious e-bike rider is pretty hilarious. I also got a big kick out of Cartman's interview scene, where his secret identity wasn't particularly well hidden.

This was definitely Cartman and Randy's week to shine. With Randy, it's just so nice to finally be rid of the played-out Tegridy Farms shtick and onto something new. It really works seeing Randy suddenly recast as a weed-hating, cycling-obsessed health nut who looks down his nose at the kids and their newfangled e-bikes. And it's only fitting that this episode takes that new role to its extreme, leading to Randy forming a violent South American biker gang that pays off the police and delivers the heads of their enemies to the mayor. I can only wonder where this strange new journey will take Randy over the course of Season 29.

It's also worth mentioning that the City Wok owner, Lu Kim, plays a pretty great supporting role here. His business has transformed yet again (though we get a fun nod to Season 27's Labubu fad on the signage), this time focusing on peddling City E-Bikes and Super City E-Bikes. The premiere's musical game is also very on-point. Not only does Brad Paisley contribute that catchy little country music ditty that closes out the episode, but Trey Parker and Matt Stone even brought in Primus to re-record the intro song for this new South America era.

On that note, the title change serves to anchor this episode to the current political climate. This is South Park's way of eviscerating Trump's habit of unilaterally renaming geopgraphic landmarks and of corporations like Apple and Google simply rolling over and embracing the name changes. As much as I'm concerned this gag is going to grow stale really quickly in Season 29, it is pretty funny to watch the news reporter take the townspeople to task for capitulating. We'll see how well this joke holds up in the coming weeks.

items.title: Tiny Fugitives Review
items.author: Scott Collura
items.content:
Tiny Fugitives is in theaters on September 18.

Is there anything sadder than a kid sitting alone in the school cafeteria?

That, in essence, is what Tiny Fugitives is about, the latest comedy that features Johnny Knoxville, but in actual fact is about a group of 12 year olds who decide that summer sleepaway camp is where they want to live for the rest of their days, because their regular lives just aren’t cutting it. Unfortunately, as heartwarming and good-natured as the film can be at times, it also suffers from a bit of an identity crisis, never really finding the balance between its dick jokes, Knoxville-as-human-target shenanigans, and more soft and gentle leanings.

The film opens with Jacob (Benjamin Pajak) at the front of his classroom, charming his fellow students as he convinces them of the magic of camp. “Fuck school!” his teacher finally yells, completely sold on his pitch. “Let’s go to camp!” The class erupts in cheers…

Except it’s all been a daydream, and in fact Jacob is the kid who has no friends, gets picked on by the class bully, and yep, eats alone in the cafeteria. And that’s why camp is so important to him, since it’s those two months of each year where he gets to really live. It’s “10 for 2,” as he and his best friend at camp, Charness (Aaron Harris), call it – 10 months of the regular year for the two months at camp. The best of times.

And really, some of the stuff these kids are dealing with does help to paint a picture of why they don’t love it back home. Charness not only doesn’t have friends either, but he claims that his parents are starting to hate him. Jacob’s folks, meanwhile, are on the verge of divorce, and generally the two boys are miserable when not at camp. So when Jacob learns that his parents might not be sending him back next summer, he and Charness devise a plan to run away to “Old Camp,” the original site of their camp where “over the pants handjobs were literally invented.” OTPHJs!

Tiny Fugitives either doesn’t know what it wants to be, or there’s not enough of it there to be just one thing.

Cute, right? And so the kids escape, with Knoxville’s over-the-hill (well, he’s 50 in the movie) camp counselor Bob soon embarking on the hunt to find them. From there, a series of setpieces involving the hijinks the kids get into – including Isa Bernal Steiner's Tali, Jai Soundar's Leon, and Alyssa Gervasi's Sophie – are intermixed with the star’s Looney Tunes-style buffoonery as each attempt to capture the kids results in him getting electrocuted, thrown from fast-moving vehicles, etc.

And really, that’s part of the problem with Tiny Fugitives. It either doesn’t know what it wants to be, or there’s not enough of it there to be just one thing. The kids having crushes on each other and learning life lessons stuff can be genuinely sweet – Leon and Sophie get mock-married at one point, with Sophie later having to break it to Leon that things aren’t going to work out since “you’re 10” – but then all of a sudden here’s Knoxville’s Bob, pursuing the gang like some kind of fannypack-wearing T-1000. It’s jarring.

(One also can’t help but notice how much Knoxville in the movie. Yes, he’s the name to get people in theater seats, and Tiny Fugitives is really about the kids in the end, but I was surprised by how few sequences actually lean into the cartoonish “hurt Bob” scenario the film seems to promise.)

Co-written and directed by Michael Lewen, Tiny Fugitives calls back to a type of movie of old that we perhaps don’t see enough of these days. Meatballs is the easy comparison, but it’s not just the summer camp aspect that I’m talking about. There’s a low-stakes, low-yield, “hey, that was fun and I’ll never think about this movie again” feel to the picture that is kind of rare in our go-big-or-go-home times. But it’s also hampered by the type of problems that a movie like that would’ve also been in danger of suffering from back in the day, namely an undercooked script, under-directed performances, and illogical character turns.

It’s a shame though, because there’s a heart beating beneath the surface of this little movie that is just waiting to come bursting to the surface. It’s like that kid sitting at the lunch table all alone – if someone would just give them a chance, they have so much potential.

items.title: The Grand Tour Reboot Season 1 Review
items.author: Luke Reilly
items.content:
All six episodes of season 1 of The Grand Tour’s new series are available to watch now on Prime Video.

At the peak of its power, The Grand Tour became Prime Video’s most-watched unscripted UK original series globally, but the show’s been up on the hoist since September 2024, when original hosts Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond, and James May took their final bow in the episode “One for the Road.” It marked the last trip for the trio after 22 years of working together on The Grand Tour and the BBC’s Top Gear. 2026’s new vision of The Grand Tour – hosted by Thomas Holland, James Engelsman, and Francis Bourgeois – is an ambitious attempt to prove that the format can soldier on without the much-loved line up that previously helmed it. Perhaps against all odds, it has mostly succeeded.

The new series’ opening moments see an awestruck new trio share a moment with Jeremy Clarkson on his Diddly Squat Farm, which is a brief sketch setting Clarkson up as something closer to a head of state than an elder peer. It’s a cute if slightly clunky bit, but it’s a smart springboard for the new series; they may be restarting from “Season 1” as far as their presence on Prime Video is concerned, but the new Grand Tour is not ignoring the series’ history. In this way, it becomes less of a reboot and more of a relay; they’re just picking up the baton and carrying on. “Seriously, have fun with this,” says Clarkson as they depart, in probably the one part of the encounter that genuinely feels off the cuff. “I mean it, and good luck. And don’t f–k it up.”

The basic formula of the show remains intact – a mix of bespoke themed segments and long-form road trips (in this instance, across parts of the US, Malaysia, and Angola). If there’s been a noteworthy reduction in budget since the departure of the original hosting trio, it’s certainly not visible on screen. The vehicle footage remains sumptuously shot, and there’s no skimping on the execution of expensive ideas, whether that’s using a giant airbag to fling an unwanted Tesla through the air and destroy it, or a hypercar race involving three jets and a £2.1 million, 2,031 brake horsepower Hennessey Venom F5 Revolution Evolution.

What’s perhaps most pleasing is the immediate rapport between all three hosts. Admittedly, Holland and Engelsman arrive from well-established YouTube motoring channel Throttle House, where their chemistry has already been developed through years of video content. It means that they’re not only comfortable in front of a camera discussing cars, they’re also comfortable disagreeing with each other, and their unplanned exchanges typically seem like credible banter between mates. Bourgeois is particularly surprising; as the one member of the new trio who come from a motoring journalism background, his inclusion was hard to figure out in the lead-up to his debut. I’m unfamiliar with his social media schtick because I’ve never used TikTok, but his enthusiasm for his new role is utterly infectious and he seems extremely knowledgeable. The show certainly leans into his established social media fascination with trains, but he knows cars too. He’s a truly interesting fellow who communicates with the quietly spoken authority of someone twice his age, but he can flip a switch and become a buzzing teenager behind the wheel… and he’s highly watchable as both.

If you want a quick taste of Bourgeois’ presenting style, you can dip in to the opening segment of Episode 4, where he and Holland pit two hideously expensive restomods against one another: a Totem GT Super (reimagining the classic Alfa Romeo GTA) and the Prodrive P25 (a half-a-million pound remake of the absolutely legendary Subaru Impreza 22B). As an absolute sucker for ’90s rally cars, I couldn’t help but share Bourgeois’ deep admiration for the P25, and the fact that it was introduced with one of the strongest needle drops I’ve heard in the show’s history didn’t hurt. One of the best rock bangers of the ’90s to celebrate one of the baddest four-bangers ever unleashed on gravel? Yes, please! It’s actually a segment they could’ve done a bit more with, considering how much the concept of restomods mirrors what’s happening with this new season. Taking a recognizable classic and updating it with new, modern internals? The script would’ve almost written itself.

Prior to the debut of the new series, Thomas Holland admitted that after hearing The Grand Tour was being rebooted without Clarkson, Hammond, or May, he quipped: “Only a moron would take that job.” The sentiment has clear precedent. For many years, the BBC’s Top Gear tried to establish a line-up of replacement hosts for the programme after Clarkson was axed and Hammond, May, and producer and co-creator Andy Wilman subsequently followed him out the door. Top Gear then saw eight different hosts from 2016 up until the show was put on ice in 2023. It became fascinated by filling the roster with sitcom stars, cricket players, and F1 team founders, and it never rediscovered the proper formula. It’s early days, but I think The Grand Tour has.

items.title: Hot Wheels Infinite Rush Review
items.author: Luke Reilly
items.content:
Giving the modern Hot Wheels racing series a radical, Burnout Paradise-inspired overhaul sounds like a pretty fabulous idea when you say it aloud. That Criterion Games classic is, after all, one of the most revered arcade racers in the business – even if it was ultimately the last proper Burnout we ever got. Unfortunately, Hot Wheels Infinite Rush has sacrificed far, far too much of what makes developer Milestone’s initial pair of Hot Wheels Unleashed games so eye-catching, zany, and special. Infinite Rush’s four modestly sized maps weave familiar bits and pieces of plastic track through otherwise unmemorable slabs of landscape and basic city blocks, and they totally lack the scope and spectacle of the Unleashed series’ life-sized skate parks, construction sites, and neon arcades. The racing may be fine and functional, but Infinite Rush is disappointingly basic and bland compared to its existing brethren, so it’s difficult to recommend over either of them.

Hot Wheels Infinite Rush is instantly recognisable as a Milestone Hot Wheels game thanks to its unmatched ability to present these car models in an uncannily photorealistic way. The cars still broadly look fantastic. From zinc to plastic, the surfaces of every model gleam with authenticity and – despite the fact it’s been this way since the first one arrived in 2021 – it still remains thoroughly impressive to me how terrific they look on screen. They just look .

[It’s] instantly recognisable as a Milestone Hot Wheels game thanks to its unmatched ability to present these car models in an uncannily photorealistic way.

Unfortunately, they no longer appear to accumulate wear and tear like they did in the Milestone’s earlier games. Upon reaching the end of a race, my cars now look just as factory fresh as they did when I started. The scratches, rubs, scuffed plastic, and kerb rash that builds up on cars in the Unleashed games is a big part of what pumps up their credibility; that is, making the cars look and feel like they’ve just tumbled down the driveway a dozen times really seats them into the maps and makes them look like actual play-worn toys. In contrast, Hot Wheels Infinite Rush feels glossy and consequence-free. Am I missing something here? A hidden setting? Was this an intentional change for Infinite Rush for some unknown reason, or a licensor change-of-heart? Whatever it was, it’s a really weird step back and I’m not a fan.

Sister from Another Blister

It appears about one-third of the options that make up the roughly 150-car roster are new, rather than recycled. This is welcome, as it certainly doesn’t make much sense to keep wheeling out the same cars when there are almost 60 years of Hot Wheels castings to choose from. That said, the garage is still weighted very heavily towards new and recent models. There’s a decent smattering of early to mid-2000s castings, including AcceleRacers, but there’s really nothing here for Gen X parents or grandparents to share with younger players. The ’70s, ’80s, and ’90s remain woefully underrepresented. I get that older players aren’t really the primary audience of a licensed Hot Wheels game, but I know that my sons’ Hot Wheels collection is like a core sample of Hot Wheels history. It’s got recent cars, my childhood cars, and old cars from their uncles – and even great uncle. I get the feeling that’s probably a pretty common occurrence. The balance in Infinite Rush is just… off. There are definitely times it feels like it was more important for this to be a catalogue of cars kids can still see at the shops rather than a rummage through the toyline’s past.

Infinite Rush is also missing the pop culture cars that were fixtures in the Unleashed games. The fact that it features Ferrari is neat enough, considering the Prancing Horse’s decade-long absence from the real-life Hot Wheels line-up from 2015 to 2025, but the lack of any movie or TV cars feels a bit cheap.

Infinite Rush uses a similar class system for the cars as Unleashed 2, although it dials it back to four distinct classes rather than six: Versatile, Speeder, Drifter, and Titan. Each has nuances you need to cater for as you drive. For instance, Titans are strong but bulky – and they have extra long boost meters to compensate. However, run your boost all the way down to zero and your default speed will be strangled momentarily as your engine coughs back to life. Versatile racers have a drift bar that’s consumed in chunks, meaning you can’t stop a boost once you’ve started. It means they’re not a great fit for navigating the urban, grid-like portions of the maps, because it can be hard to force them into the right direction when in the middle of a briefly unstoppable boost.

Drifters are my preferred class, since they’re the easiest to sling sideways and therefore the best fit for an arcade racing game. The other classes are less satisfying to drift, and there sometimes seems as if there’s even a bit of a speed penalty for doing so. There were definitely occasions it was overtly faster to Hail Melon around a corner, Ross Chastain-style, than it was to slide into it properly. This shouldn’t really be the case in any arcade racer.

The biggest problem with Infinite Rush is how surprisingly generic the open-world approach makes it feel. It doesn’t have a single, large open map to explore like, say, Burnout Paradise or Forza Horizon 6. Instead, there are four separate, modestly sized islands – each themed in slightly different ways. There’s Wheelswood, a commercial-style, downtown-inspired map; Tentacle Bay, another city-oriented environment, only with a little more open countryside; Gearville, a desert-themed, industrial zone; and Drifty Temples, an East Asian-inspired island. I just find myself blazing through them, smashing through bushes and benches. There’s some decent imagination on display – and I do think the huge Hot Wheels Mount Rushmore on Gearville is pretty cute – but broadly speaking there’s just not much that grabs my attention. Not even the big, plastic animals.

In the Unleashed games, you find yourself racing through half-built skyscrapers above the clouds – or staring up at enormous arcade cabinets, which might as well be skyscrapers themselves with the way they loom over your tiny toy cars, from down on the sticky carpet. Infinite Rush has absolutely none of this scale, and it’s all the worse for it. They’re not quite believable dioramas, even if they’re filled with moulded plastic props. But they’re not quite real places either – even if the default measure of distance to my next waypoint is metres. 800 metres away, in a car that’s ostensibly three inches long? Something’s not adding up.

In a word, these maps are bland. You just drive back and forth across them, competing in a genre-typical range of event types. The racing is still fine, although the tracks are nowhere near as interesting anymore because they simply can’t use their surroundings in the same way as the Unleashed games can. There you can race on the floors, across the furniture, up in the air vents – you name it. Infinite Rush has none of that. Worse, a lot of the side activities that appear to be here to justify these open-world maps are just busywork – like photograph challenges that tell you exactly where to take them, or checkpoint collections that’d be a lot less trivial to complete if you actually had to dodge traffic (which you don’t; smashing through them doesn’t even really slow you down).

[In the Unleashed games] you can race on the floors, across the furniture, up in the air vents – you name it. Infinite Rush has none of that.

There was probably a way to experiment and take the series to an open world without sacrificing the sense of scale Unleashed got so right. Could the desert map have been built on a beach, or one of the other maps laid out in the foyer of a toy store? Anything like this would’ve given the backdrops the scale Infinite Rush lacks. Could more of the architecture have been household objects, with cereal box buildings standing side by side with Hot Wheels garage playsets, and painted roads filling the gaps between the iconic orange track pieces? I just feel like there was a more imaginative way to tackle this shift. 2023’s LEGO 2K Drive did this approach better overall, but unfortunately that game is already completely delisted in digital stores.

The profound shift in map philosophy is doubly disappointing considering the improvements Infinite Rush makes elsewhere. For instance, it now comes with four-player splitscreen, which would’ve been amazing fun in the massively more imaginative Unleashed maps. It also now features the ability for AI to race on your custom tracks, which would’ve been another huge boost to longevity for the older games. I would’ve loved to have seen how the AI handled the wild leaps of the crazy routes I’ve created in the past (especially since Infinite Rush is way, way more restrictive in terms of the height limit than the Unleashed games – which feature multi-level maps with a ton of vertical space). Infinite Rush also features the new ability to change out wheels as part of the customisation suite, which speaks to me as a 40-odd-year-old diorama-building dork who loves swapping out wheels on his Hot Wheels cars. Okay, they’re not always mine, but my boys aren’t using them anymore; just don’t tell them I’ve been attacking their collection with a power drill.

items.title: Stranger Things: Tales From ’85 Season 2 Review
items.author: Arnold T. Blumberg
items.content:
Stranger Things: Tales From ’85, Netflix’s animated series spin-off of their Stranger Things live-action series, returns for a Valentine’s Day-themed season set in early February 1985. After , Nikki Baxter (Odessa A’zion) is now a full-fledged member of Dustin’s (Braxton Quinney) Hawkins Investigators Club or HIC. He remains the ever-enthusiastic adventurer dedicated to their club even though nightly group hunts for the weird and supernatural have unearthed nothing. But Hawkins doesn’t stay quiet for long — a petty robbery at the Palace Arcade coincides with the disappearance of town delinquent Charlie Dandridge (Benjamin Valic) and a field of ominous bioluminescent flowers popping up in the woods.

Intrigued, the HIC quickly discover that the flowers are actually Audrey II-looking critters being harvested by glowing blue “hate sprites,” as dubbed by Max, and they’re friendly. In fact, they’re harbingers of a bigger ghost-like creature that’s on the hunt for humans. Across the eight episodes of this season, the kids will determine why they’ve shown up, how they tie into the lore of Hawkins’ founding, and deal with some other unfinished business from last season.

On the character front, the impending romantic holiday brings out the worst in Max (Jolie Hoang-Rappaport), who picks plenty of fights with Lucas (Elisha “EJ” Williams), which ties into their canon on again/off again status referred to in Season 3 of the live-action series. Eleven (Brooklyn Davey Norstedt) and Mike (Luca Diaz) also continue to figure out what they are, even though Eleven remains as fiercely protective of Mike as ever.

Stranger Things: Tales From ’85 Season 2 is more focused on the core crew of characters and integrates Nikki nicely into the friend dynamic. Parents don’t factor into their late-night roamings, and even Steve Harrington is MIA. While the new mystery involves some unknown town history and an important character from Season 1, overall the scripts continue to pale in comparison to the live-action series. Characterization is kept simple, with problems stemming from one-note issues like financial troubles in Nikki’s household or Max being upset with her absent father. Instead of trying — or being allowed — to fill in the blanks with this ensemble, the majority of the season is just interested in moving the plot along or setting up big action beats. While an animated series is usually the medium for big ideas to be brought to life, this second season is an example of “more is more.” It’s actually a bit exhausting to watch fight after fight and chase upon chase when we know the core kids are safe from anything serious happening to them because of where these stories live in the timeline.

Season 2 makes it more clear than ever that a season-long mystery of even a truncated eight episodes feels too long. The set pieces remain frustratingly winnable and repetitive, while the characters only advance in minuscule ways. In truth, Stranger Things: Tales From ’85 might have been better conceived as a “case of the week” series à la Scooby-Doo, Where Are You!, where each episode was more focused on the kids pairing up for individualized creative mysteries tailored to the tone and personalities of the characters. Unfortunately, this current format is not meeting the high writing standards of the Stranger Things franchise.

Stranger Things: Tales From ’85 Season 2 isn’t so much a sophomore slump as it is a status quo continuation of the good and the less-than-great from Season 1.

Where it excel is in the quality of its animation. Flying Bark Productions executes some very cool creatures this season with the sprites, ethereal bugs, and a “Big Bad” that is striking to see in action. The animated performances of each of the cast members also remain strong and in keeping with their live-action counterparts. Jolie Hoang-Rappaport as Max and Braxton Quinney as Dustin remain the vocal MVPs, adding a lot of energy to the season even when the story gets stuck in ruts or unnecessary side missions.

Stranger Things: Tales From ’85 Season 2 isn’t so much a sophomore slump as it is a status quo continuation of the good and the less-than-great from Season 1. This season’s mystery is a little more interesting, but it doesn’t have the kind of emotional weight or originality in story we expect from this franchise.

items.title: Slow Horses Season 6, Episode 1 Review — 'Circle of Life'
items.author: Leanne Butkovic
items.content:
This review contains full spoilers for Season 6, Episode 1, which is streaming on Apple TV now.

It’s the return of Slow Horses (along with a )! The questions looming over this new six-episode season were how well it would fare after losing its creator and head writer, Will Smith, while tackling two of Mick Herron’s Slough House novels instead of one. So far, Slow Horses seems the same as ever, even if it’s maybe trying a little too hard to prove that it knows how the show’s schtick is supposed to go. Even so, it’s hard to be too nitpicky with a series that cranks out new seasons like clockwork and reliably hits its marks.

“Circle of Life” sets up the chessboard of this season’s central mystery, which sees the Slow Horses being targeted. Someone’s picking off the flunky MI5 spies from Slough House; two former agents — who both seemed to be living quiet, unglamorous lives after the service — have been killed by an unidentified twosome (played by Andor’s Kyle Soller and The Witcher’s MyAnna Buring). The current roster also seems to have been entirely wiped from the Park’s systems, and their paychecks have stopped coming too. In protest, the greasy Jackson Lamb (Gary Oldman) goes on “strike,” which mostly means departing to the Italian restaurant below Slough House and uncorking a bottle of red wine before noon.

Diana Taverner (Kristin Scott Thomas), now comfortably First Chair after outsting the bumbling Claude Whelan at the end of Season 5, seems to have had a hand in Slough House’s expungement, though isn’t cleanly admitting to anything. Among all of this early drama, River Cartwright (Jack Lowden, maybe soon to graduate from shoddy spy to good spy) is grappling with — rather, trying to completely smother — the grief from the off-camera death of his struggling grandpa, David (Jonathan Pryce), as he plans the funeral.

The disturbing opening shot of Season 6 is a statement as much as it is a metaphor for the disregard of some lives: Slow Horses, now written by the show’s longtime co-executive producer Gaby Chiappe, is still . Chiappe might not have the same comedy writing background as Smith (who worked on shows like The Thick of It and Veep) that gave the show a certain edge, but Slow Horses still .
